handbookData.text: Developing an algorithmic intuition, learning how to decompose complex tasks, converting English specifications into logic structures, and mastering code dry runs.
0.1 Algorithmic Intuition

Programming is not about syntax; it is about decomposition. An algorithm is a sequence of unambiguous, finite steps that transforms inputs into outputs. High-level problem solving requires identifying the inputs, outputs, and constraints of a system before writing a single line of code.
0.2 Breaking Problems Down

When presented with a complex problem (e.g. validating a Sudoku board), do not write code immediately. Deconstruct it: 1. Verify rows (are there duplicate numbers?). 2. Verify columns. 3. Verify 3x3 grids. By resolving these sub-problems independently, you compile a complete solution.
0.3 Pseudocode & Dry Running

Pseudocode bridges natural language and code. It describes logic without worrying about language-specific compile constraints. Dry running is tracing code execution step-by-step using a pen and paper, keeping track of variable states inside a simulation table.
Summary
An algorithmic mindset prioritizes problem decomposition, clear logic formulation, and systematic dry runs over immediate code writing.
Interview Questions

handbookData.question: "What is a dry run and why is it important?"
handbookData.answer: "A dry run is the manual tracing of an algorithm's execution on paper using sample inputs. It is crucial because it helps identify logic errors, off-by-one bugs, and boundary condition failures before compilation."

Common Mistakes
"Jumping straight into code without defining constraints or input variations."
"Not dry running code on empty or single-element boundary inputs."
Contest Tips
"In competitive programming, spend 40% of your time on paper design; coding is the easy part."

The history and compilation model of C++, installing tools, setting up compilers, standard input/output streams, variables, types, and basic operators.
1.1 History and Architecture of C++

Created by Bjarne Stroustrup in 1979 at Bell Labs, C++ extends C with object-oriented capabilities. C++ is a compiled, statically typed language, offering direct hardware access and low-level memory control, making it the dominant language in game engines, high-frequency trading, and competitive programming.
1.2 Compilation Model & Code Structure

Unlike interpreted languages (Python), C++ code is compiled directly into machine code. A compiler (like g++ or clang++) compiles source files (.cpp) into object files (.o) and links them into an executable. Let's see a standard competitive programming template:
Summary
C++ combines high-level abstractions with direct memory access. Compilation produces optimized native code, supported by fast input-output streams.
Interview Questions

handbookData.question: "What does ios_base::sync_with_stdio(false) do?"
handbookData.answer: "It disables synchronization between C++ standard streams (cin/cout) and C standard streams (scanf/printf). This dramatically speeds up I/O, preventing timeouts in competitive programming."

Visualizing iterations with for/while loops, pattern recognition math, deriving grid formulas, and dry running patterns.
2.1 Loop Visualization & Matrix Grids
Loops repeat instructions. Nested loops represent multi-dimensional coordinate grids where the outer loop iterates over rows (i) and the inner loop iterates over columns (j).
2.2 Pattern Clue Formula Derivation

To print any pattern, represent row index i (0-based) and column index j (0-based), then derive a boolean formula for whether to print an asterisk or space. Let's draw a right-angled triangle of size N:
2.3 Hourglass & Custom Star Loops
For complex shapes like butterflies or hourglasses, split the pattern into upper and lower halves, derive formulas for spaces and stars independently, and execute loops.
Summary
Grid patterns are created by mapping outer loops to rows and inner loops to columns, using coordinate formulas to determine character output.

handbookData.question: "How do you print a hollow square of size N?"
handbookData.answer: "Use nested loops from 0 to N-1. Print an asterisk if it's on the boundary (i == 0 || i == N-1 || j == 0 || j == N-1), otherwise print a space."

Static array memory layout, basic operations (searching, rotation, reversing), multidimensional coordinate grids, Matrix Calculator, and Sudoku Validator.
3.1 Array Memory Layout

An array is a contiguous block of memory holding elements of the same type. Because elements are sequential, access is O(1) via base address calculations: Address(A[i]) = BaseAddress + i * sizeof(type).
3.2 Matrix Rotations and Grids

2D arrays are stored in row-major order in memory. A common matrix operation is rotating a matrix 90 degrees clockwise in-place. This is achieved by: 1. Transposing the matrix (swapping element [i][j] with [j][i]). 2. Reversing each row.
3.3 Project: Sudoku Validator
A Sudoku validator checks if a 9x9 grid satisfies rules: no duplicates in any row, column, or 3x3 sub-grid. We use arrays of boolean flags to track digits 1-9 in O(1) space.
Summary
Arrays store contiguous sequences. Multidimensional arrays are mapped to contiguous memory in row-major order. In-place rotation combines transpose and reverse steps.
Interview Questions

handbookData.question: "Why is dynamic size array access (std::vector) preferred over static array (int arr[N]) in contests?"
handbookData.answer: "std::vector manages memory dynamically on the heap, preventing Stack Overflow errors if array size is huge, and supports convenient member functions like resize(), size(), and push_back()."

C-style character arrays vs std::string, frequency counting hash structures, checking palindromes, text analyzers, and password validators.
4.1 std::string vs Character Arrays

C-style strings are null-terminated character arrays (`char str[]`) ended by `�`. std::string is a dynamic class container that handles memory automatically. Reversing, copying, and comparing strings are O(N) operations.
4.2 Frequency Hashing
Many string problems (e.g. check anagrams) are solved in O(N) time using frequency counts. We map characters to indices in a 26-size integer array: index = char - 'a'.
4.3 Project: Text Analyzer
A text analyzer reads words, counts unique word frequencies, detects occurrences of specific search words, and masks sensitive characters.
Summary
std::string provides dynamic sizing. Frequency counting uses a fixed size array of 26 to achieve O(N) anagram verification.
Interview Questions

handbookData.question: "What is the difference in memory layout between char* and std::string?"
handbookData.answer: "char* is a raw pointer containing the memory address of a null-terminated character array. std::string is a wrapper class containing a pointer to dynamically allocated heap memory, the length of the string, and capacity details."

Solve these curated problems to consolidate your understanding:

"Problem 2: Longest Common Prefix - Find the longest shared prefix among an array of strings."

"Access string characters in O(1) using index notation s[i]."
"Always check for string boundaries; s.length() is unsigned (size_t)."
Common Mistakes
"Running s.length() - 1 in a comparison when s is empty, causing integer underflow (since size_t is unsigned)."
"Concatenating strings inside loops using s = s + char, which makes a full string copy O(N^2); use s += char instead (O(N) amortized)."
Contest Tips
"In string contests, use string::clear() and reserve() to avoid continuous re-allocations."

handbookData.title: Sorting, Searching & Binary Search on Answer

handbookData.text: Linear vs Binary Search, Ternary Search, Binary Search on Answer optimization, Bubble/Selection/Insertion sorts, Merge/Quick/Heap sorts, and non-comparison sorts.
5.1 Binary Search & Binary Search on Answer

Binary search cuts the search space in half O(log N) but requires sorted data. Binary Search on Answer is an advanced technique used when the search space is monotonic: if a condition holds for value X, it also holds for all values > X (or < X). We binary search the range of possible answers, validating correctness at each step.
5.2 Classical Sorting Algorithms
Sorting arranges items in order. We distinguish Comparison sorts (Bubble, Selection, Insertion: O(N^2); Merge, Quick, Heap: O(N log N)) and Non-Comparison sorts (Counting, Radix, Bucket: O(N + K)).
Summary
Binary Search runs in O(log N) time. Binary Search on Answer explores monotonic decision spaces, and non-comparison sorting (Counting Sort) breaks O(N log N) limits.
Interview Questions

handbookData.question: "When is Merge Sort preferred over Quick Sort?"
handbookData.answer: "Merge Sort is stable and has a guaranteed O(N log N) worst-case time complexity, making it ideal for sorting linked lists or memory-constrained database files. Quick Sort is in-place (O(log N) space) but has a worst-case complexity of O(N^2) if the pivot choices are poor."

handbookData.text: Practice Problems
Solve these curated problems to consolidate your understanding:
"Problem 1: Koko Eating Bananas - Find the minimum speed to eat all bananas within H hours using Binary Search on Answer."
"Problem 2: Merge Sort - Implement Merge Sort from scratch on a vector."
Revision Notes
"Binary search mid formulation: mid = low + (high - low) / 2 prevents integer overflow."
"Stable sorting preserves the relative order of duplicate elements."
Common Mistakes
"Using binary search on an unsorted array, returning incorrect index coordinates."
"Writing mid = (low + high)/2 which can overflow if low and high are large integer indices."
Contest Tips
"If the problem constraints mention 'maximize the minimum' or 'minimize the maximum', think Binary Search on Answer."

Understanding physical addresses, pointers, references, dynamic heap allocation, passing mechanics, and memory leaks.
6.1 Address Space & Pointer Dereferencing
A pointer is a variable that stores the memory address of another variable. The address-of operator `&` extracts the address, and the dereference operator `*` accesses the value at that address.
6.2 Dynamic Memory Allocation (Heap)

Memory allocated on the stack is cleaned up automatically when the function returns. Dynamic memory is allocated on the heap using the `new` operator and must be freed manually using the `delete` operator (or `delete[]` for arrays) to prevent memory leaks.

handbookData.code:
int* ptr = new int(10); // Allocate space for single int on heap
std::cout << *ptr << "\n";
delete ptr;             // Free memory
ptr = nullptr;          // Prevent dangling pointer

int* arr = new int[100]; // Allocate array on heap
delete[] arr;           // Free array memory

handbookData.text: 6.3 Pass by Value vs Reference vs Address
• **Pass by Value**: Copies the argument. Modifying parameters does not affect originals.
• **Pass by Reference**: Passes an alias. Modifying parameter modifies the original. Efficient for large classes.
• **Pass by Address (Pointer)**: Passes pointer address copies. Allows modifying original and passing nullptr values.
Summary
Pointers store addresses of physical memory. Stack objects auto-deallocate, while heap variables require explicit delete calls to prevent memory leaks.
Interview Questions

handbookData.question: "What is a memory leak and how do you prevent it?"
handbookData.answer: "A memory leak occurs when a program allocates memory on the heap using new but fails to release it using delete. To prevent leaks, always use smart pointers (std::unique_ptr, std::shared_ptr) which automatically manage resource release."

handbookData.text: Practice Problems
Solve these curated problems to consolidate your understanding:
"Problem 1: Swap Pointers - Write a function using pointers to swap two integer values."
"Problem 2: Dynamic Vector - Create a resizeable dynamic array using raw pointers."
Revision Notes
"References cannot be reassigned or be null; pointers can be reassigned and hold nullptr."
"Double free errors happen when delete is called on the same pointer twice."
Common Mistakes
"Dangling pointers: accessing a pointer after deleting its heap address."
"Forgetting to delete[] for arrays allocated with new[], causing resource leaks."
Contest Tips
"Set pointers to nullptr immediately after calling delete to avoid accidental re-access."
Further Reading

7.1 Big O, Theta, and Omega Definitions
• **Big O (O)**: Upper bound. Describes the worst-case resource execution scaling limit.
• **Big Omega (Omega)**: Lower bound. Describes the best-case execution scale limit.
• **Big Theta (Theta)**: Tight bound. Describes worst and best case bounds simultaneously.
7.2 Loop Complexity Analysis
Complexity is determined by counting operations as input N scales:
7.3 CP Constraint Constraints Rules
Summary
Time complexity analysis bounds code steps under input scaling. Contest constraint limits guide target algorithm choice.
Interview Questions

handbookData.question: "What is the space complexity of a recursive function that has maximum depth D?"
handbookData.answer: "The space complexity is O(D) due to the recursive call stack memory frames. Each active recursive call adds a frame to the stack holding arguments and local states."

Mastering C++ containers (vector, stack, queue, map, set), iterators, and algorithms (sort, lower_bound, upper_bound).
8.1 STL Containers Overview

The Standard Template Library (STL) provides optimized, ready-to-use data structures. We group them into Sequence (vector, list, deque), Container Adapters (stack, queue, priority_queue), and Associative (set, map, unordered_set, unordered_map) containers.
8.2 STL Algorithms & Bounds
• `std::lower_bound`: Returns iterator to the first element >= target. O(log N).
• `std::upper_bound`: Returns iterator to the first element > target. O(log N).
Summary
STL simplifies structure implementation. std::set is implemented as a Red-Black tree (O(log N)), whereas std::unordered_set is a Hash Table (O(1)).
Interview Questions

handbookData.question: "What is the difference between map and unordered_map?"
handbookData.answer: "std::map is sorted and implemented using red-black trees, yielding O(log N) lookup and insertion. std::unordered_map is unsorted and uses hash tables, yielding O(1) average operations, but has a worst-case complexity of O(N) if hash collisions occur."

"Problem 2: Count Frequencies - Count word frequencies in a text using unordered_map."
Revision Notes
"Use reserve() on vectors to prevent expensive dynamic memory reallocations."
"lower_bound returns iterator to >= target; upper_bound returns > target."
Common Mistakes
"Using std::unordered_map with custom keys without defining a hash function."
"Calling lower_bound(s.begin(), s.end(), x) on std::set. This runs in O(N) because iterators are non-random access; use s.lower_bound(x) instead, which runs in O(log N)."
Contest Tips
"In Codeforces, avoid unordered_map if possible, or use custom hashes to prevent anti-hash tests causing O(N^2) collisions."

Efficient range sum queries using 1D and 2D prefix sums, and updating intervals with Difference Arrays.
9.1 1D Prefix Sum Queries

For an array A, its prefix sum array P is defined as P[i] = P[i-1] + A[i]. It allows computing range sum queries over query range [L, R] in O(1) time: Sum(L, R) = P[R] - P[L-1] (using 1-based indexing).
9.2 Difference Arrays (Range Updates)

If we need to add value X to all elements in range [L, R] repeatedly, we can use a Difference Array D. For each update, we perform D[L] += X and D[R+1] -= X. The final array is computed by taking prefix sums of D, reducing range updates to O(1) time.
Summary
Prefix sum arrays reduce range queries to O(1). Difference arrays handle range updates in O(1) time by modifying boundary values.
Interview Questions

handbookData.question: "Explain the formula for a 2D Prefix Sum range query."
handbookData.answer: "For a 2D grid, the range sum of a sub-rectangle from (r1, c1) to (r2, c2) is: Sum = P[r2][c2] - P[r1-1][c2] - P[r2][c1-1] + P[r1-1][c1-1]. The final term is added back because it is subtracted twice by the other sub-grids."

"Problem 2: Corporate Flight Bookings - Apply difference arrays to perform range updates."

"Difference arrays only yield values after a final prefix sum pass."
Common Mistakes
"Forgetting to allocate size N + 1 for difference array boundaries, causing buffer overflows when R = N-1."
"Using 1-based indexing without adjusting L-1 indices."
Contest Tips
"Use prefix sums when there are queries but no updates; use Segment Trees if updates occur."

Fixed and variable size sliding global optimization techniques, maximum sum subarray, and longest substrings.
10.1 Fixed Size Window

The sliding global pattern converts nested loops O(N^2) into linear passes O(N) when evaluating contiguous subarrays. In a fixed global of size K, we compute the result of the first global, then shift the global by adding element R and removing element L on each step.
10.2 Variable Size Window
In variable-sized windows, we expand pointer R to find valid windows and contract pointer L when constraints are violated, tracking the maximum or minimum global length.
Summary
Sliding windows maintain contiguous subarray states. Pointers expand (R) and contract (L) to calculate optimal constraints in O(N) time.
Interview Questions

handbookData.question: "When should you use Sliding Window instead of Two Pointers?"
handbookData.answer: "Sliding Window is a specific subset of the Two Pointers pattern, used when we evaluate contiguous segments (subarrays/substrings) of an array. General Two Pointers can evaluate non-contiguous elements (e.g. comparing start and end values in a sorted array)."

Base 2 conversions, bitwise operators (AND, OR, XOR, NOT), unique number queries, subset generation, and bitmasking.
11.1 Bitwise Operators & Masking
Computers store integers in binary. Bitwise operations run directly on CPU registers in a single cycle:
• `&` (AND): Sets bit to 1 if both inputs are 1. Clear bit: x & ~(1<<i).
• `|` (OR): Sets bit to 1 if either input is 1. Set bit: x | (1<<i).
• `^` (XOR): Sets bit to 1 if inputs differ. properties: x ^ x = 0, x ^ 0 = x.
11.2 Subset Generation using Bitmasking
An array of size N has 2^N subsets. We can represent subsets using binary numbers from 0 to 2^N - 1, where the i-th bit indicates if element A[i] is present in the subset:
Summary
Bit manipulation enables single-cycle CPU operations. Bitmasks represent subsets, mapping set inclusions to active bit bits.
Interview Questions

handbookData.question: "How do you check if an integer is a power of 2 in O(1) time?"
handbookData.answer: "An integer X is a power of 2 if and only if X > 0 and (X & (X - 1)) == 0. Subtraction flips all bits after the lowest set bit, so their bitwise AND is exactly zero."

Prime numbers, Greatest Common Divisor, Least Common Multiple, the Sieve of Eratosthenes, modular arithmetic rules, and fast exponentiation.
12.1 Primes & Sieve of Eratosthenes

A prime number has no divisors other than 1 and itself. Checking if a number is prime takes O(sqrt(N)) time. To find all primes up to N, the Sieve of Eratosthenes runs in O(N log log N) time by marking multiples of each discovered prime.
12.2 Fast Exponentiation & Modular Inverse

Calculating (A^B) % M using naive loops takes O(B) time, which is too slow. Fast Exponentiation (Binary Exponentiation) computes this in O(log B) time by squaring the base recursively: if B is even, A^B = (A^(B/2))^2; if B is odd, A^B = A * (A^(B-1)).
Summary
The Sieve of Eratosthenes finds primes in O(N log log N). Fast Exponentiation squares bases recursively to calculate modulo powers in O(log B).
Interview Questions

handbookData.question: "What is Fermat's Little Theorem and how does it calculate modular inverse?"
handbookData.answer: "Fermat's Little Theorem states that if M is prime, then A^(M-1) = 1 (mod M). Multiplying both sides by A^-1 yields A^-1 = A^(M-2) (mod M). Thus, modular inverse can be calculated using fast exponentiation with power M-2."

Recursive thinking patterns, base case formulation, Call Stack frames, and analyzing recursion trees.
13.1 Recursive Thinking

Recursion is a process where a function calls itself. A valid recursive function must contain: 1. Base Case: The termination condition that returns a value directly. 2. Recursive Step: Decomposing the problem into a smaller sub-problem of the same nature.
13.2 Call Stack & Recursion Tree

Every recursive call creates a stack frame in system memory, storing local variables and return paths. A Recursion Tree visualizes execution splits, showing time complexity as the sum of work done at all tree levels.
The recursion tree for Fibonacci has depth N and branches twice per step, resulting in O(2^N) time complexity and O(N) call stack space.
Summary
Recursion breaks problems down into smaller sub-problems. Every call is tracked on the system Stack. Call trees visualize O(2^N) execution splits.
Interview Questions

handbookData.question: "What is Tail Recursion?"
handbookData.answer: "Tail recursion occurs when the recursive call is the absolute last operation executed by the function. Modern compilers can optimize tail recursion by reusing the current stack frame, reducing call stack space to O(1)."

Formulating state space trees, N-Queens problem, subset generation, and solving Sudoku puzzles dynamically.
14.1 State Space Search & Pruning

Backtracking is a search algorithm that explores a State Space Tree systematically, building candidate solutions step-by-step and backing up (backtracking) as soon as it determines a candidate cannot yield a valid complete solution (pruning).
14.2 N-Queens Implementation
The N-Queens problem seeks all layouts of N non-attacking queens on an N x N chessboard. We use backtracking to place queens row by row, checking column and diagonal conflicts:
Summary
Backtracking systematically searches state spaces. Placements are validated recursively, and states are reverted during step backtrack phases.
Interview Questions

handbookData.question: "How does pruning improve backtracking efficiency?"
handbookData.answer: "Pruning stops recursive exploration of a branch as soon as constraints are violated (e.g. finding a queen collision). This avoids evaluating millions of invalid state leaves, saving massive compute."

Opposite direction pointer patterns (Pair Sum, Palindromes) and same direction sliding comparisons.
15.1 Opposite Direction Pointers

Two pointers is a pattern where two indices iterate over an array simultaneously. In the opposite direction pattern (e.g. checking 2-sum in a sorted array), pointers start at indices 0 (L) and N-1 (R). We evaluate the sum: if it's too small, we increment L; if it's too large, we decrement R, reducing O(N^2) loops to O(N).
15.2 Same Direction Pointers
Pointers start at the same boundary and shift at different speeds (e.g. fast/slow pointers for linked list cycle detection, or merging sorted arrays).
Summary
Two Pointers run in O(N) time. Pointers start at opposite edges and converge based on sorting comparisons, avoiding nested loops.
Interview Questions

handbookData.question: "Why does the opposite pointer technique require a sorted array?"
handbookData.answer: "Because the movement logic depends on monotonic ordering. If the sum is smaller than target, we only increment L because that guarantees a larger sum. If the array were unsorted, incrementing L could increase or decrease the sum, destroying the logic."

16.1 Node Memory Structs

Unlike arrays, linked list nodes are stored in non-contiguous heap locations, containing value data and pointers to neighbor nodes. Access is sequential O(N); insertion and deletion are O(1) once the node address is located.
16.2 Reversing a Linked List
Reversing a singly linked list is performed in O(N) time and O(1) space by rearranging pointer arrows using three pointers: `prev`, `curr`, and `next`:
16.3 Cycle Detection (Floyd's Tortoise & Hare)
To detect a cycle in a linked list, run two pointers: slow (moves 1 node per step) and fast (moves 2 nodes per step). If a cycle exists, they will eventually meet inside the loop.
Summary
Linked lists link nodes via pointers. Reversing is executed by flipping next-pointer targets, and loops are detected using slow/fast pointers.

handbookData.question: "Why is Floyd's Cycle Detection space complexity O(1)?"
handbookData.answer: "It only uses two pointers (slow and fast) to traverse the list nodes, requiring zero auxiliary memory tables, unlike hash-set methods which require O(N) space."

LIFO Stack mechanics, FIFO Queue operations, Deques, Monotonic stacks (finding next greater element), and Expression Evaluators.
17.1 LIFO vs FIFO
• **Stack**: Last-In-First-Out (LIFO) container. Push and pop occur at the top. O(1) operations.
• **Queue**: First-In-First-Out (FIFO) container. Push at back, pop at front. O(1) operations.
• **Deque**: Double-Ended Queue. Supports push and pop at both front and back in O(1) time.
17.2 Monotonic Stack (Next Greater Element)
A monotonic stack maintains elements in sorted order (increasing or decreasing). It is used to find the next greater element in O(N) total time, by popping elements smaller than the current value:
Summary
Stacks follow LIFO; queues follow FIFO. Monotonic stacks pop smaller elements to calculate next-greater relations in linear time.
Interview Questions

handbookData.question: "What is a Monotonic Queue and when is it used?"
handbookData.answer: "A Monotonic Queue maintains elements in a sliding global in sorted order. It is used to find the minimum or maximum element in all sliding windows of size K in O(N) time (e.g. Sliding Window Maximum problem)."

Tree definitions, depth-first vs breadth-first tree traversals, Binary Search Trees properties, and computing diameter and LCA.
18.1 Tree Traversal (DFS vs BFS)

A tree is a connected, acyclic graph. In a binary tree, each node has at most two children. DFS traversals visit nodes recursively: Pre-order (Root-L-R), In-order (L-Root-R), and Post-order (L-R-Root). BFS (Level-order) visits nodes layer by layer using a FIFO queue.
18.2 Binary Search Trees (BST)

A BST satisfies: for any node, all left subtree keys are smaller, and all right subtree keys are larger. This properties allows searching in O(H) time, where H is the tree height. An In-order traversal of a BST returns keys in sorted order.
18.3 Diameter & Lowest Common Ancestor (LCA)
• **Diameter**: The longest path between any two leaf nodes. Computed recursively: Max(LeftDiameter, RightDiameter, LeftHeight + RightHeight).
• **LCA**: The deepest node that is ancestor to both target nodes.
Summary
BFS uses queues; DFS uses recursion. BSTs partition keys for O(H) search, and In-order traversals of BSTs output elements in sorted order.
Interview Questions

handbookData.question: "How do you balance a Binary Search Tree?"
handbookData.answer: "Standard BSTs can degenerate into O(N) linked lists. Balanced BSTs (AVL Trees, Red-Black Trees) use rotation operations during insert/delete to maintain height H = O(log N)."

handbookData.title: Heaps, Priority Queues & Top K Problems

handbookData.text: Binary heaps, array representations, heapify logic, implementing std::priority_queue, and solving Top K elements.
19.1 Binary Heap Array Representation
A binary heap is a complete binary tree stored compactly in an array. For a node at index i (0-based):
• Left child index = 2 * i + 1
• Right child index = 2 * i + 2
• Parent index = (i - 1) / 2
In a Max-Heap, the parent key is >= children keys. Heapify maintains this constraint by bubbling elements up or down, running in O(log N) time.
19.2 C++ std::priority_queue & Top K
C++ uses priority_queue (max-heap by default). We solve Top K largest elements in O(N log K) time using a Min-Heap of size K, popping smallest values if size exceeds K:
Summary
Heaps map trees to array indices. Heapify maintains heap properties, and min-heaps extract Top K elements in O(N log K) time.
Interview Questions

handbookData.question: "What is the time complexity of building a heap from a raw array of N elements?"
handbookData.answer: "Building a heap (Build-Heap) from a raw array takes O(N) time using Floyd's heap construction algorithm (running heapify bottom-up), not O(N log N) which occurs if we push items one-by-one."

20.1 Trie Node Structure

A Trie (prefix tree) is a multi-branch tree structure used to store strings. Each node represents a character, branching to children representing subsequent characters. Tries search prefix strings in O(L) time where L is the query length, independent of word counts.
20.2 Insertion & Search
20.3 Project: Auto Suggestion System

handbookData.question: "Compare Trie and Hash Map for dictionary search."

21.1 Greedy Choice Property

A greedy algorithm makes the locally optimal choice at each step with the hope that these local choices lead to a globally optimal solution. To prove a greedy algorithm works, we use Proof by Contradiction or Exchange Arguments.
21.2 Interval Scheduling

Given N meetings with start and end times, schedule the maximum number of non-overlapping meetings. The greedy choice is: always select the meeting that ends earliest. Sorting meetings by end times takes O(N log N) time:
Summary
Greedy algorithms make locally optimal choices. Sorting by earliest end times yields optimal interval selections in O(N log N) time.

handbookData.question: "Why does sorting by earliest start times fail for interval scheduling?"

Memoization vs Tabulation, space optimization, state and transition designs, and classic DP patterns.
22.1 DP Core Framework: State & Transition

Dynamic Programming (DP) solves optimization problems by combining solutions to overlapping sub-problems. The DP framework requires: 1. State Design: Defining what DP[i] represents (e.g. maximum profit at step i). 2. Transition Design: Finding the mathematical recurrence mapping current state to previous states.
22.2 Memoization (Top-Down) vs Tabulation (Bottom-Up)
• **Memoization**: Uses recursion to solve sub-problems and caches results. Easy to write but has recursive stack overhead.
• **Tabulation**: Uses loops to fill tables bottom-up. Faster, bypasses stack limits, and enables space optimization.
22.3 0/1 Knapsack Tabulation with Space Optimization
22.4 Advanced DP Patterns

We categorize DP patterns: 1. LIS (Longest Increasing Subsequence). 2. LCS (Longest Common Subsequence). 3. Knapsack. 4. Grid Path. 5. Tree DP. 6. Bitmask DP (representing visited states as bit integers). 7. Digit DP.
Summary
DP optimizes overlapping sub-problems. Tabulation bypasses recursion stack limits, and rolling arrays compress O(N * W) space to O(W).
Interview Questions

handbookData.question: "Why do we loop backwards (W down to wt[i]) in the space-optimized 0/1 Knapsack?"
handbookData.answer: "Looping backwards ensures that we compute the current item's state using sub-problem states from the previous iteration. If we looped forward, we would overwrite early states, allowing an item to be selected multiple times (which is Unbounded Knapsack)."

handbookData.title: Graphs: BFS, DFS, Shortest Paths & MST

handbookData.text: Graph representations, BFS/DFS sweeps, Dijkstra, Bellman-Ford, Floyd-Warshall, Kruskal, Prim, DSU, and advanced connectivity.
23.1 Graph Traversals (BFS & DFS)

Graphs are represented as Adjacency Lists (`vector<int> adj[N]`). DFS uses recursion (Stack) to explore paths deep before backtracking. BFS uses a Queue to explore neighbors layer by layer, finding shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
23.2 Dijkstra's Shortest Path Algorithm

Dijkstra finds shortest paths from a source node to all nodes in a weighted graph with non-negative edge weights. It runs in O((V + E) log V) time using a min-priority queue to select the node with the minimum distance and relax its outgoing edges:
23.3 Disjoint Set Union (DSU) & MST

DSU (Union-Find) manages partitions of elements, supporting Union and Find queries in near-constant O(alpha(N)) time using path compression. Kruskal's algorithm uses DSU to build a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) by sorting edges and adding non-cyclical edges.
Summary
BFS finds unweighted shortest paths; Dijkstra resolves weighted non-negative shortest paths using priority queues. DSU coordinates MST edge checks in Kruskal.
Interview Questions

handbookData.question: "When must you use Bellman-Ford instead of Dijkstra?"
handbookData.answer: "Bellman-Ford must be used if the graph contains negative edge weights. Dijkstra fails because it assumes paths can only grow longer. Bellman-Ford runs in O(V * E) time, relaxing all edges V-1 times, and can detect negative weight cycles."

24.1 Segment Tree Architecture

A Segment Tree is a binary tree where each node stores compiled information (sum, min, max) of a subarray range. It processes range queries and point updates in O(log N) time, requiring O(N) array allocation space.
24.2 Segment Tree Implementation
24.3 Lazy Propagation

When updating ranges of elements, updating each element individually takes O(N log N) time. Lazy Propagation optimizes this by delaying child updates. The parent node caches update data in a lazy tree and applies it only when children are accessed, reducing range updates to O(log N).
Summary
Segment Trees partition arrays into logarithmic ranges. Lazy propagation defers node updates, facilitating O(log N) range alterations.

handbookData.question: "Why do we allocate size 4N for a Segment Tree of size N?"
handbookData.answer: "A Segment Tree is a full binary tree. If N is a power of 2, the leaf nodes require N slots and internal nodes require N-1 slots, totaling 2N-1. If N is not a power of 2, the tree height expands, requiring up to 4N slots in array representation."

29.1 The Five-Step Interview Framework
A technical interview is not just a coding test; it is a collaborative design session. Follow the framework:
1. **Understand**: Read the problem aloud, clarify assumptions (e.g. duplicates? negative numbers?), and state constraints.
2. **Brute Force**: Describe the naive solution immediately. Explain its time/space complexity (e.g. O(N^2)), setting a baseline.
3. **Optimize**: Discuss optimization steps (e.g. using hash map to reduce search times, sorting first, dynamic tables).
4. **Code**: Write clean, modular C++ code. Use descriptive variable names and helper functions.
5. **Test**: Dry run your code using sample inputs on paper. Walk through lines systematically, tracking variable values.
29.2 Communication & Whiteboarding
Never remain silent. Talk out loud. The interviewer wants to evaluate your reasoning. If you go silent for > 2 minutes, they cannot assess your skills, even if your final code is correct.
Summary
FAANG prep focuses on a five-step framework: clarify constraints, present brute force, optimize, code cleanly, and dry run inputs.

handbookData.question: "How do you handle an unseen problem during an interview?"
handbookData.answer: "Don't panic. Clarify constraints. Run simple examples manually to identify patterns. Compare it with similar problems (e.g. using the Pattern Recognition system). Suggest a brute-force approach to get started, and interact with the interviewer for guidance."

A rigorous 7-step blueprint to analyze, design, optimize, code, and test any DSA problem systematically.
31.1 The Seven-Step Blueprint
To solve unseen problems under constraints, follow a structured framework:
1. **Understand**: Parse inputs, outputs, and sample cases. Ask: 'Is the array sorted?', 'Are there negative weights?'
2. **Evaluate Constraints**: Check limits (N). Determine if target complexity is O(N), O(N log N), or O(2^N).
3. **Brute Force**: Write down the naive nested-loop solution. Evaluate its complexity.
4. **Optimize**: Look for redundancy. Can we cache states? Can we use sliding windows? Can we binary search?
5. **Pattern Match**: Cross-reference keywords and constraints with the Pattern Recognition system.
6. **Implement**: Code the solution cleanly. Handle boundaries (empty arrays, single nodes) first.
7. **Verify**: Dry run edge cases manually. Compare with brute force output.
Summary
The 7-step problem-solving framework guarantees logical consistency, avoiding runtime errors and ensuring optimized complexity.
Interview Questions

handbookData.question: "How do constraints guide optimal algorithm choice?"
handbookData.answer: "If N <= 10^5, an O(N^2) solution will TLE. The algorithm must run in O(N log N) or O(N) time. If N <= 20, an O(2^N) backtracking solution is perfectly acceptable, avoiding unnecessary complex structures."

Blueprints, structures, and algorithms for building: Search Engines, Auto-completes, Social Networks, and Student Ranking Engines.
32.1 Project 1: High-Speed Search Engine

A search engine indexes millions of documents. We represent the vocabulary using an Inverted Index (implemented as `std::unordered_map<string, vector<int>>` mapping words to document IDs). To support search queries, we use set intersections (Two Pointers) on document ID lists, returning ranked results in O(D) time.
32.2 Project 2: Auto-Complete System

Auto-complete displays suggestions as a user types. We construct a Trie (Prefix Tree) storing words with frequencies. When a prefix is input, we navigate to the prefix node and query a max-priority queue to retrieve the Top K most frequent completions.
32.3 Project 3: Social Network Graph

A social network models user friendships as an Undirected Graph. We use Adjacency Lists to store friendships. Breadth-First Search (BFS) is executed to find degree-of-separation paths, and Dijkstra is used to route weighted post distribution feeds.
32.4 Project 4: LearnXChain Student Ranking Engine

The LearnXChain student ranking engine tracks leaderboard positions of thousands of active programmers. The architecture combines three structures: 1. `std::unordered_map` for O(1) score updates. 2. A Policy-Based Ordered Set (`ordered_set`) to evaluate student ranks in O(log N) using `order_of_key`. 3. A Segment Tree to track score distribution percentiles dynamically.
Summary
Real products build on DSA primitives. Tries suggest completions, inverted index structures power search queries, and ordered sets index student leaderboards.
Interview Questions

handbookData.question: "Why is an adjacency list preferred over an adjacency matrix for social networks?"
handbookData.answer: "A social network graph is extremely sparse (users have hundreds of friends out of millions). An adjacency matrix requires O(V^2) space, which consumes terabytes of memory. Adjacency lists require O(V + E) space, storing only active connections, maximizing efficiency."

34.2 DP Transition Recurrences Cheat Sheet
• **Fibonacci**: DP[i] = DP[i-1] + DP[i-2]
• **0/1 Knapsack**: DP[w] = max(DP[w], Val[i] + DP[w - Wt[i]])
• **LIS**: DP[i] = max(1, 1 + DP[j]) for all j < i if Arr[j] < Arr[i]

Interview Questions

handbookData.question: "Why does vector push_back have O(1) amortized time complexity?"
handbookData.answer: "A vector allocates capacity blocks. When the array fills up, it doubles its size and copies elements, which is an O(N) operation. However, since this doubling happens rarely (exponential intervals), the average cost per push_back is O(1)."
